Maximum Likelihood Covariance Matrix and Means of Incomplete Data

Source: R/cov_fiml.R
cov_fiml.Rd

For continuous variables some of whose values are missing, cov_fiml() returns the maximum likelihood estimates of their covariance matrix and mean vector under the multivariate normal model, computed from every observed value rather than from the complete cases alone. These are the estimates of the saturated (unrestricted) model fitted by full information maximum likelihood (FIML), the model in which every variance, covariance, and mean is free. They are computed by the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm of Dempster, Laird, and Rubin (1977) and are often called the EM covariance matrix and the EM means (Enders & Peugh, 2004). The function requires lavaan, whose EM implementation does the computing.

The usual alternatives each give something up. Listwise deletion keeps only the complete cases, and its estimates are consistent in general only when values are missing completely at random (MCAR). Pairwise deletion estimates each covariance from a different subset of cases, so the matrix need not be positive definite and has no single sample size (Marsh, 1998). The EM estimates use every case and are consistent when values are missing at random (MAR) given the variables in the model (Schafer & Graham, 2002). They are therefore the matrix to hand to a method that starts from a covariance or correlation matrix, such as an exploratory factor analysis or a parallel analysis of incomplete items.

Usage

cov_fiml(data, aux = NULL)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or numeric matrix of continuous variables, with missing values coded NA. Every column that aux does not name is an analysis variable, a row and column of the returned S. Every column must be numeric; a factor, character, or logical column is refused, as is a column with fewer than two distinct observed values.

aux

Optional character vector naming auxiliary columns of data: variables that are not wanted in S but carry information about the missing values, because they predict which values are missing, the missing values themselves, or both. They enter the saturated model with the analysis variables, so their information reaches S and mu, and are then left out of what is returned (the saturated correlates treatment of Graham, 2003, the one the reliability family's aux argument uses).

Value

A list with the same six elements whatever the data. A matrix is what every use of the result takes (stats::cov2cor(), stats::factanal(covmat = ), a function's S argument), so the result holds the matrix itself, as cov_sem and covmat_from_cfa return theirs, rather than a table of its elements:

S

The maximum likelihood covariance matrix of the analysis variables (divisor N), with their names as row and column names, in the order of the columns of data.

mu

The maximum likelihood mean vector of the analysis variables, named, in the same order.

N

The number of cases used: those with at least one observed value among the analysis variables and the auxiliaries.

N_complete

The number of cases observed on every analysis variable.

patterns

The number of distinct patterns of observed and missing values among the cases used, over every variable in the saturated model (the analysis variables and the auxiliaries); missing_patterns tabulates them.

converged

TRUE when the EM algorithm met its convergence criterion.

Details

What is estimated. With complete data the estimates are the sample moments with the maximum likelihood divisor: S equals cov(data) * (N - 1) / N and mu equals colMeans(data). With missing values, the EM algorithm alternates two steps until the estimates stop changing. The expectation step fills in the sums and cross products each case would contribute, replacing a missing value by its regression prediction from the observed values of its case under the current estimates and adding the residual covariance to the cross products; the maximization step recomputes the moments from those sums. No iteration lowers the likelihood of the observed data. Meeting the stopping criterion establishes numerical stability of the iterations, not a finite global maximum or uniqueness. The estimates are those of the unrestricted (h1) model of every FIML fit in lavaan: lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "sampstat.h1") returns them for a model fitted with missing = "ml" to the same variables. cov_fiml() computes them with lavaan's EM (lavaan::lavCor() with missing = "ml") and its default convergence criterion, which stops the iterations when no mean or covariance changes by more than \(10^{-5}\). That is a criterion on the absolute change, and in the units of variables whose standard deviations are near .001 it is met after an iteration or two, far from the maximum. cov_fiml() therefore runs the algorithm on the variables centered at their means and divided by their standard deviations, each computed from the variable's observed values, and transforms the estimates back, so that they do not depend on the units: multiplying a variable by a constant multiplies its mean, and its row and column of S, by that constant. They agree with lavaan's own estimates of the same moments to the precision of the criterion, about seven significant digits. When the algorithm stops at its iteration limit instead, converged is FALSE, a warning says so, and S and mu are the last iterate rather than the maximum likelihood estimates.

When the estimates are consistent. The estimates are consistent when the values are MAR given the variables in the saturated model: the probability that a value is missing may depend on the observed values of the variables included, but not on the missing values themselves (Schafer & Graham, 2002). MAR is defined relative to the variables analyzed (Enders, 2001). If whether an item is missing depends on a variable that is left out, MAR need not hold for the items alone, and naming that variable in aux brings it back into the model without making it part of S. Including such variables (the inclusive strategy) costs little and can remove a bias that leaving them out would leave in place (Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). Under missingness that depends on the missing values themselves (not at random), no choice of auxiliaries guarantees consistency. Normality enters as the working likelihood: Yuan, Yang-Wallentin, and Bentler (2012) summarize results showing that the normal theory estimates can remain consistent when the population distribution is unknown, and their simulations found the normal theory variance estimates biased at smaller sample sizes when the data were not normal, a bias that shrank as the sample grew.

Cases used. A case on which every variable, analysis and auxiliary, is missing carries no information and is set aside, as lavaan would set it aside. Every other case is used, including a case whose analysis variables are all missing but whose auxiliaries are observed. Under MAR given an auxiliary, such cases carry the auxiliary values of exactly the people whose analysis variables are missing, which is how the model learns how those people differ, and setting them aside would pull the estimates back toward those of the cases that responded. N counts the cases used and N_complete the cases complete on the analysis variables, all that listwise deletion would keep.

Refusals. Two variables that are never observed together have a covariance the data say nothing about: the likelihood is flat in that direction, and an EM estimate of it reflects the starting values and the other covariances rather than the data. The same holds, in substance, for two variables observed together only in rows where one of them takes a single value (or in one row only): those rows say nothing about how the two vary together, and the estimate of their covariance rests on the form of the normal model, or is not determined at all when one of them is observed nowhere else. The function refuses either kind of pair and names it; missing_coverage reports the number of cases behind every pair.

Using the matrix downstream. N is the number of cases used, not an effective sample size, and the matrix carries less information than N complete cases would. A method that takes a covariance matrix and a sample size and treats them as complete data gets consistent point estimates from S, but its standard errors and test statistics are too optimistic, because they ignore the information the missing values took away (Savalei & Bentler, 2009). Enders and Peugh (2004) studied which sample size to give such a method when fitting a confirmatory factor model: the smallest number of cases behind any covariance gave Type I error rates near the nominal level when every indicator had missing values (the smallest number behind any variance did when only some indicators had them), and the harmonic mean of the numbers behind the variances gave confidence intervals with coverage near the nominal level. missing_coverage reports the number of cases behind every variance and covariance. The two-stage approach of Savalei and Bentler (2009) corrects the standard errors and the test statistic of a model fitted to the EM moments (lavaan's missing = "two.stage"), and a model fitted to the raw data by FIML needs no correction. The fraction of missing information (fraction_missing_information) says what the missing values cost each parameter of such a fit. For point estimates, such as the eigenvalues of a factor analysis or of a parallel analysis, the EM matrix is the consistent basis.

Standard errors. The function returns point estimates only. The sampling variability that matters is that of whatever is computed from the matrix, and the analysis that computes it is where its interval belongs.

References

Collins, L. M., Schafer, J. L., & Kam, C.-M. (2001). A comparison of inclusive and restrictive strategies in modern missing data procedures. Psychological Methods, 6(4), 330–351. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.6.4.330

Dempster, A. P., Laird, N. M., & Rubin, D. B. (1977). Maximum likelihood from incomplete data via the EM algorithm. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series B (Methodological), 39(1), 1–38.

Enders, C. K. (2001). A primer on maximum likelihood algorithms available for use with missing data. Structural Equation Modeling, 8(1), 128–141.

Enders, C. K., & Peugh, J. L. (2004). Using an EM covariance matrix to estimate structural equation models with missing data: Choosing an adjusted sample size to improve the accuracy of inferences. Structural Equation Modeling, 11(1), 1–19.

Graham, J. W. (2003). Adding missing-data-relevant variables to FIML-based structural equation models. Structural Equation Modeling, 10(1), 80–100. doi:10.1207/S15328007SEM1001_4

Marsh, H. W. (1998). Pairwise deletion for missing data in structural equation models: Nonpositive definite matrices, parameter estimates, goodness of fit, and adjusted sample sizes. Structural Equation Modeling, 5(1), 22–36. doi:10.1080/10705519809540087

Savalei, V., & Bentler, P. M. (2009). A two-stage approach to missing data: Theory and application to auxiliary variables. Structural Equation Modeling, 16(3), 477–497. doi:10.1080/10705510903008238

Schafer, J. L., & Graham, J. W. (2002). Missing data: Our view of the state of the art. Psychological Methods, 7(2), 147–177. doi:10.1037/1082-989X.7.2.147

Yuan, K.-H., Yang-Wallentin, F., & Bentler, P. M. (2012). ML versus MI for missing data with violation of distribution conditions. Sociological Methods & Research, 41(4), 598–629. doi:10.1177/0049124112460373

See also

missing_patterns and missing_coverage to describe the missing values first; fraction_missing_information for what they cost the parameters of a FIML fit; reliability_alpha and reliability_omega, whose missing = "fiml" paths also bring auxiliary variables into a saturated model.

Other missing data: df_barnard_rubin(), df_missing(), fraction_missing_information(), missing_coverage(), missing_patterns()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu

Examples

# The six spatial tests of the Holzinger and Swineford data. The revised
# paper form board (t25) and flags (t26) tests were given only at
# Grant-White, so the 156 Pasteur pupils are missing both of them.
spatial <- c("t1_visual_perception", "t2_cubes", "t3_paper_form_board",
             "t4_lozenges", "t25_paper_form_board_r", "t26_flags")
em <- cov_fiml(holzinger_swineford[spatial])
em$N
#> [1] 301
em$N_complete
#> [1] 145
em$patterns
#> [1] 2
round(stats::cov2cor(em$S), 2)
#>                        t1_visual_perception t2_cubes t3_paper_form_board
#> t1_visual_perception                   1.00     0.30                0.37
#> t2_cubes                               0.30     1.00                0.24
#> t3_paper_form_board                    0.37     0.24                1.00
#> t4_lozenges                            0.44     0.34                0.31
#> t25_paper_form_board_r                 0.40     0.33                0.41
#> t26_flags                              0.47     0.21                0.31
#>                        t4_lozenges t25_paper_form_board_r t26_flags
#> t1_visual_perception          0.44                   0.40      0.47
#> t2_cubes                      0.34                   0.33      0.21
#> t3_paper_form_board           0.31                   0.41      0.31
#> t4_lozenges                   1.00                   0.31      0.49
#> t25_paper_form_board_r        0.31                   1.00      0.30
#> t26_flags                     0.49                   0.30      1.00

# Listwise deletion would keep the 145 Grant-White pupils alone and
# estimate every correlation from them.
round(stats::cor(holzinger_swineford[spatial], use = "complete.obs"), 2)
#>                        t1_visual_perception t2_cubes t3_paper_form_board
#> t1_visual_perception                   1.00     0.33                0.37
#> t2_cubes                               0.33     1.00                0.19
#> t3_paper_form_board                    0.37     0.19                1.00
#> t4_lozenges                            0.45     0.42                0.37
#> t25_paper_form_board_r                 0.40     0.31                0.40
#> t26_flags                              0.47     0.23                0.33
#>                        t4_lozenges t25_paper_form_board_r t26_flags
#> t1_visual_perception          0.45                   0.40      0.47
#> t2_cubes                      0.42                   0.31      0.23
#> t3_paper_form_board           0.37                   0.40      0.33
#> t4_lozenges                   1.00                   0.33      0.47
#> t25_paper_form_board_r        0.33                   1.00      0.30
#> t26_flags                     0.47                   0.30      1.00

# Values missing at random given a variable that is not analyzed: word
# meaning (t9) goes missing more often for pupils who scored high on
# general information (t5). The two visual tests say little about those
# pupils, so without t5 the mean of t9 stays near that of the pupils who
# took it; named as an auxiliary, t5 recovers most of the difference.
set.seed(113)
d <- holzinger_swineford[c("t1_visual_perception", "t4_lozenges",
                           "t9_word_meaning", "t5_general_information")]
z <- as.numeric(scale(d$t5_general_information))
p_missing <- stats::plogis(-0.5 + 2 * z)
d$t9_word_meaning[stats::runif(nrow(d)) < p_missing] <- NA
without_aux <- cov_fiml(d[1:3])
with_aux <- cov_fiml(d, aux = "t5_general_information")
rbind(without_aux = without_aux$mu, with_aux = with_aux$mu,
      full_data = colMeans(holzinger_swineford[names(d)[1:3]]))
#>             t1_visual_perception t4_lozenges t9_word_meaning
#> without_aux             29.61462    18.00332        12.42404
#> with_aux                29.61462    18.00332        14.66152
#> full_data               29.61462    18.00332        15.29900
